articles.title: The New Spider-Man Is Pure Fun
articles.author: Eileen Jones
articles.content: What can be said about a new Spider-Man movie besides, in a tone of incredulity, “It’s another one!”Well, a few things. Spider-Man: Brand New Day was directed by Destin Daniel Cretton, who also did Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings (2021), which I enjoyed. It was lighthearted and humorous, with excellent action sequences and nice low-key character work, and it made a movie star, briefly, of Simu Liu. I’d like to see more movies with Simu Liu, by the way, and I don’t mean when he’s playing bit parts like one of the Kens in Barbie (2023), or one of the crowd of Avengers, as he will be in his return as Shang-Chi in the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday. It’s nice that he’s making a living and all, but the way Hollywood wastes charismatic charm is a sin and a shame.Young stars getting much more career cosseting are Tom Holland and Zendaya, who return for the fourth entry in this latest rebooted Spider-Man series, after the trilogy Spider-Man: Homecoming (2017), Spider-Man: Far from Home (2019), and Spider-Man: No Way Home (2021). Playing Spider-Man/Peter Parker and his snarky beloved Michelle “MJ” Jones-Watson in this start of a new trilogy — my gods, it’s relentless — Holland and Zendaya are reaching a professional zenith after their much-publicized marriage and their performances in the epic hit The Odyssey, which opened just a few weeks ago and is still showing on rival screens.They’re both far better in Spider-Man: Brand New Day. That squeaky-clean nice-guy tenor in a gee-whiz American accent adopted by Holland — who’s a Brit — in order to play Peter Parker is odd and distracting when he’s enacting the role of Telemachus, prince of Ithaca, the callow son of Odysseus, but it’s just right as part of the cartoon fun of Spider-Man movies. And Zendaya is, of course, beautiful, but playing the goddess Athena as Christopher Nolan wrote her, as a glumly concerned onlooker with nothing goddess-y to do, did not serve her. She’s wonderfully modern in affect and has nice comic timing. She and Holland have a relaxed bantering style together that’s sweet and entertaining.The best thing about Spider-Man: Brand New Day is that it’s not trying to be anything more than gleeful fun, packing high-energy action, frequent laughs, and plenty of emotive drama into a polished entertainment package. There’s very little of that silly fake profundity you have to put up with when certain directors who shall remain nameless take over a superhero movie. And it’s already a colossal hit, setting a box-office record on opening day that beats another box-office record previously set by a Marvel movie, Avengers: Endgame (2019).Spider-Man: Brand New Day follows up on the plot ending from the last of these movies, efficiently summed up in a few lines appearing in the opening credit imagery, when Dr Strange (Benedict Cumberbatch) cast a spell making the world forget the identity of Peter Parker, which had leaked out with potentially disastrous consequences. The result is that Spider-Man can go on efficiently fighting crime in New York City with nobody knowing his true identity. But that includes the people in Peter’s personal life — girlfriend MJ and their former MIT classmate and pal Ned Leeds (Jacob Batalon) included.Since his supportive aunt May (Marisa Tomei) has died as a result of her connection to Spider-Man, Peter now lives a life of monkish isolation dedicated only to his lonely pursuit of dangerous baddies. His most intimate connection is the police detective Jean DeWolff (Liza Colón-Zayas), who talks to him on the phone about the latest heists and dangers to the public thoroughfares.This is a superhero plot we’ve seen a million times — the figure idolized by the public for his unbeatable speed, strength, and constant heroics who’s nevertheless living a life of abject misery and alienation, and must find his way back to some sort of basic human connection in order to save himself. We like the dark romance of this character, just like we are endlessly diverted by stories of movie stars who seem to have everything — beauty, money, fame, adulation — but are revealed to have been deeply troubled and unhappy all along.The trials of Peter Parker/Spider-Man don’t end there, though. He’s also got a potentially deadly problem that’s arising from his angst, which is the spiking of stress-related arachnid hormones in his system, making his spidery qualities erratic and excessive. Suddenly he’s shooting spiderwebs out of his wrists, not his suit, and he can’t control the quantities — sometimes nothing spurts out, sometimes it’s web in such profusion he’s waking up cocooned in it, hanging off the edges of buildings.He experiments with scientific fixes, and there are amusing scenes of trial and error as he lurches and plummets and blasts off wildly all around the city. But it’s a bad time to lose control of his powers, because there’s a mysterious new force of mayhem at work in New York, an invisible human-possessing force that can jump rapidly from person to person, causing each person to flop back and forth when overtaken or abandoned, like one of those wildly waving inflatable tube men advertising used cars or something. So Spider-Man has no idea who this apparent foe is, as he’s repeatedly confronted by some random person on the street looking at him mockingly, challenging him to keep up, and saying witheringly, “You are a simple spider.”Meanwhile, there’s plenty of time for Peter/Spidey to moon around tracking MJ and Ned and feeling extra sad. This is made easier by Ned’s always-online presence and Spider-Man fandom, which includes his invention of a smartphone “Spidey-Tracker,” which will come in useful at various points.There’s top talent popping out all over in this film, which is one of the long-standing pleasures of Hollywood genre movies — tremendously gifted actors showing up in small roles giving casually terrific performances. Florence Pugh is, as always, fabulous as Yelena Belova/Black Widow, here playing a few scenes humorously lounging in a spa pool she calls “my office” and dismissing the small potatoes — no, make that the “leetle baby potatoes” — that Spider-Man concerns himself with while the Avengers deal with global “big potatoes” problems. Somehow the light, pop quality of the character makes Pugh’s extraordinary acting gifts even more startling than when she’s playing a more demanding role.Mark Ruffalo brings all kinds of shadings to his Bruce Banner/Hulk performance because he’s apparently a mensch who never just phones it in before collecting his enormous payment for a few scenes. And Sadie Sink of Stranger Things has a major role I can’t describe because it’s a spoiler, but she’s very effective. TV talent is strongly represented here, with Tramell Tillman bringing his enigmatic qualities over from Severance, and Liza Colón-Zayas of The Bear doing remarkably heartwarming work in a generic good-cop role.The one performance I could’ve done without was Jon Bernthal’s Frank Castle/Punisher, whose macho vigilantism is so broad stroke in its belligerence, it became annoying that Peter/Spidey keeps trusting him. Bernthal — who was also in The Odyssey, playing Menelaus as a vengeful brute — seems to turn up everywhere these days, enacting variations on toxic masculinity. Not Bernthal’s fault he has that broken-nosed roughneck look, I guess, but what a way to make a living!But if you’re looking for totally undemanding entertainment, there are a number of pleasantly distracting aspects of Spider-Man: Brand New Day to keep you going through the movie’s very long, typically plot-laden running time. You’ve got to remember not to let your mind wander, however — above all, don’t think about the dire state of cinema or the even more dire state of the world while you watch.Because if you love movies, this endless superhero movie juggernaut is, and has long been, exhausting and depressing because it sucks up all the money, talent, energy, and press coverage, leaving leftover crumbs for all the other potentially more ambitious cinematic endeavors. And if you let yourself dwell on the enormous resources dedicated to these distracting cinematic circuses we attend when we’re in the midst of about six different deadly global crises that threaten all life on earth, you’ll feel ill thinking what all that money could do if we weren’t constantly, willfully, flushing it all away.And that definitely won’t help you stay engaged in how Spider-Man will catch the body-hopping menace, or whether Peter Parker will ever get up the nerve to tell MJ about their lost love.Sometimes, we’ve got to admit, we’re dying for some idle distraction.

articles.title: The Cuban Revolution Was a Revolution in Art and Culture
articles.author: Abel Prieto
articles.content: As part of the Rumbo a Cuba , a Cuba solidarity mission — in which, for the first time, a civil society vessel crossed the Atlantic Ocean carrying solar energy equipment for a pediatric hospital in Havana — Jacobin contributor Simón Vázquez visited Abel Prieto at Casa de las Américas. A writer and essayist, former minister of culture of Cuba, and today president of this institution founded by Cuban revolutionary Haydée Santamaría, Prieto has been one of the central figures of the Cuban Revolution’s cultural policy for more than three decades. He chaired the National Union of Writers and Artists of Cuba (UNEAC), twice headed the Ministry of Culture, and served as an adviser to both Fidel and Raúl Castro. In this discussion with Jacobin , Prieto takes stock of the cultural legacy of the Cuban Revolution, its errors — from the Padilla affair to the anti-gay repression of the Military Units to Aid Production (UMAP) — and the challenges of Cuba’s present: the blackouts, emigration, social media, and the battle over meaning. Simón Vázquez Let’s start at the beginning. How would you characterize the Cuba you came of age in, prerevolutionary Cuba? Abel Prieto Remember that we were a colony of the Yankees for sixty years. In 1898, they intervened in Cuba to rob us of our victory over Spain, and then they seized the island and turned it into a neocolony. Cuba was where the neocolonial model made its debut: for the first time they built a false republic in the country — with the money, with political control and economic control. Here the most important figure was the United States ambassador: he was the voice of the master. Our bourgeoisie was not properly national, as in other Latin American countries; it was a bourgeoisie that looked obsessively to the north. It sent its children to study in the north, and it tried to consume all the cultural junk that came from the north and to parrot it. It was a bourgeoisie that despised the African roots of our identity. Just imagine trying to understand Cuba while despising the African component: it’s impossible. The entire spiritual legacy of our country’s African roots, which is enormously rich — they regarded as the devil’s work. What they consumed was their made-in-the-USA culture. It was in that context, the context of a new Cuba, that I was formed. Simón Vázquez Faced with that criollo bourgeoisie that despised all things African, what did the revolution do with that legacy? Abel Prieto From very early on, the revolution gave great standing to the African cultural and spiritual legacy, which is essential to understanding this country. The National Theater helped place the National Folkloric Ensemble, in terms of artistic prestige, on the level of the National Ballet of Cuba: the Frenchified, white, bourgeois ballet, suddenly on the same footing as the dance, movement, and music of black Cubans. Before the revolution, ballet was like an ornament of the bourgeois family — the little girl playing piano and learning her dance steps. Suddenly it became an expression of a new, mixed-race national culture. There were great mestizo dancers: our own Carlos Acosta — they’re stars. Simón Vázquez You worked very closely with Fidel Castro. On the centenary of his birth, his relationship with culture and the intelligentsia hasn’t been the most-discussed side of him. What kind of relationship did he build with Cuban intellectuals? Abel Prieto The relationship Fidel created with Cuban intellectuals is unique. In 1961, with the speech “Words to the Intellectuals” (“Palabras a los intelectuales”), he had founded a cultural policy that had no precedent in any revolutionary process. From the Fourth Congress on, he “moved into the Union [the National Union of Writers and Artists of Cuba],” as people say: he didn’t miss a single meeting of the national council, didn’t miss a single congress, spent the whole time listening to people, taking part in the debate. Fidel loved intellectual debate. That caricature of Fidel as a dictator who listened to no one, who imposed his own criteria, is false and indefensible. Fidel was a great intellectual — though perhaps he wouldn’t have liked being called one — who relished debate. Simón Vázquez And on a terrain as thorny as race? Abel Prieto There in the UNEAC, several black actors and actresses put it to Fidel that we still had racial prejudice in Cuba. Out of that discussion came, in my judgment, Fidel’s most important speech on the racial question. Fidel explained how, at the start of the revolution, he and the revolutionary leadership had believed that by liquidating the institutional barriers of racism — doing away with whites-only beaches, the institutional, formal side — the problem would be solved; racism would dissolve. And he said that he was now coming to understand that it is a cultural problem, a complex problem, even if solving that kind of problem was slower. Out of those discussions, he began asking about the skin color of art students, of social workers; he deliberately promoted greater participation by dark-skinned people. Che Guevara had already said it: the university has to be painted the colors of the worker, the peasant, the black, the mulatto. Simón Vázquez That drive to democratize culture — how did it dodge both Soviet socialist realism and North American mass culture at the same time? Abel Prieto Fidel was an enemy of elite culture. But at the same time, from 1961 on, he rejected the Soviet model of didactic, simplifying realism — the kind that turned art into propaganda, until in the end it worked neither as propaganda nor as art — and he also rejected the Yankee model of mass culture, the idea of stereotypes, the good guys and the bad guys, the mediocre, Manichaean, simplified vision of the world. Fidel allied himself with the intellectual vanguard. Simón Vázquez Can you give a concrete example of that? Abel Prieto He invented a television program he called University for All . The first course was a workshop on narrative technique taught by a great Cuban writer, now deceased — a workshop for young writers that he’d been giving to a tiny group — and Fidel turned it into something massive: he put it on television. Each course came with a booklet, a tabloid printed on newsprint, sold for a few cents at the kiosks, with print runs of half a million copies. The interesting thing, when you ask how many people actually learned to write narrative from that course, is that it wasn’t many. But what it did promote, in an incredible way, was reading, because people went to the library, to the bookstore, to look for the books mentioned in the course. Simón Vázquez It was a cultural prescription. Abel Prieto That too. There’s the key to escaping simplification, whether of the Soviet or the Yankee stripe: put the vanguard front and center, ally yourself with the vanguard. Fidel was convinced that people could be prepared to understand and enjoy any kind of artistic or literary expression: the key lies in education and culture. For him — he said it a thousand times — without culture there is no possible freedom. It’s the idea of culture and emancipation, a Martían idea: José Martí said that to be cultured was the only way to be free. Fidel said that without culture there is no possible freedom, because you can be manipulated. Simón Vázquez Do you see that mechanism at work today, with the rise of the New Right? Abel Prieto We’re seeing it today, with the rise of fascism, with these elections in Latin America. In a speech at the University of Havana in November 2005, Fidel analyzes what he calls the conditioned reflex. He says: imperialism says, “Cuba is bad, socialism is bad,” and off go the wretched of the earth behind it — those with no job, no education, no public health — repeating, “In Cuba, socialism . . . ” and they do it without thinking, without analyzing, by conditioned reflex. That’s what’s happening today with social media. In that speech, in my opinion, Fidel anticipates the debate over social media, the idea that people stop analyzing, stop thinking, and instead react to a stimulus with hatred, with rage, or with contempt, by conditioned reflex. Simón Vázquez Fidel spoke of the “right-wing poor.” Abel Prieto It worried him: poor people handing their vote to a demagogue because they’ve been manipulated. It’s a phenomenon we have in abundance: you have it in Spain, all over Latin America, in Europe, in the United States. Many people voted for Jair Bolsonaro in Brazil — people from the favela, humble people — and Bolsonaro was never going to look out for the fate of their families. Fidel said that only education and culture could guarantee you the ability to think for yourself, independently. Simón Vázquez You were saying that in culture, too, one can regress. Abel Prieto There can be regression: you can’t treat it as conquered territory. When the Cuban National Press was created, Fidel said: We don’t tell the people “believe,” we tell them “read.” We’re not interested in producing fanatics; we’re interested in producing cultured, free people. And this country became a country of readers. Here we published Fyodor Dostoevsky in print runs of twenty thousand or fifty thousand copies, all the great Russian literature; but also Benito Pérez Galdós, Victor Hugo’s Les Misérables , and the great literature of the United States, from Mark Twain to Gore Vidal. Today people read less and less, all over the world. We’ve regressed. Simón Vázquez An example of that regression? Abel Prieto Baseball, which is part of Cubans’ cultural heritage, and today young people are into soccer. This World Cup is a frenzy among the youngest. It makes sense that they’d share in that global appeal, because we live in the famous global village. But we’re losing something very important. Baseball is a slower sport, one that demands that you understand it, that you analyze it; and today people have no capacity for concentration. Simón Vázquez In the midst of the crisis, what role do social media and that nostalgia for 1950s Cuba play? Abel Prieto Because of the great offensive of mass idiotization, we have a very large emigration of young people, driven mainly by economic motives but also cultural ones: they’ve bought the fairy tale of the golden kingdom of prosperity in the United States. One of the things being done on social media is to idealize the Cuba of the past, the Cuba before the twenty-first century. There are tons of AI-generated videos of 1950s Havana, the Havana of glamour: a kid in the middle of a blackout suddenly sees a glamorous Havana, full of lights, of cars, of neon, Tropicana, the Hollywood stars. On one side, there’s the lack of information — we have to teach history — and on the other there are the new codes. Simón Vázquez And is anyone responding in those same codes? Abel Prieto There are very interesting initiatives using reels, those little one-minute videos. I saw one I liked a lot that uses a Bad Bunny song called “Lo que le pasó a Hawaii” (What Happened to Hawaii): the thesis of a very young, mixed-race kid is “we don’t want what happened to Hawaii to happen to Cuba.” There’s a really promising path there for getting young people interested in an issue, coming at it through music they like. But the challenge is enormous: a Cuban teenager is under the influence of the phone twenty-four hours a day. Simón Vázquez Let’s return to “Words to the Intellectuals.” Sixty-five years have passed since that founding speech of cultural policy, which held that the Cuban Revolution would not have one specific artistic form, as socialist realism was, and which sorted artists into three categories: revolutionary artists, counterrevolutionary artists, and nonrevolutionary artists. What was the most important thing about that speech? Abel Prieto It’s a subject I’m passionate about. That speech goes so far as to say that we can only renounce those who make themselves incorrigibly reactionary, incorrigibly counterrevolutionary. That word is tremendous: “incorrigible.” The idea that a counterrevolutionary might set himself straight. And he always says “if he is honest”: the idea of honesty, of ethics — that a counterrevolutionary might rectify, might draw closer to the revolution. Fidel says the revolution must have room for a nonrevolutionary artist and guarantee that artist’s space of creative freedom. There he was answering a Catholic writer who asked whether he would have the freedom to express his faith, and Fidel told him yes — that it was about opening a space to work for the revolution, with the revolution, in freedom. Fidel doesn’t put labels on art; he speaks to the creators. “Words to the Intellectuals” is a call for the most generous, the broadest unity, acknowledging diversity and the great cultural work the revolution has ahead of it. Fidel even says something to the writers and artists: we want you to create for the people, but not to make concessions on quality, because we have to work with the people so that they can understand, enjoy, and absorb your creation, however complex it may seem. That’s why the betrayal of “Words to the Intellectuals” from 1971 onward was so bitter. Simón Vázquez “Words to the Intellectuals” was put forward as the revolution’s cultural policy, and years later came a turn in the opposite direction — the notorious “gray five-year period” and its censorial turn, the well-known Padilla affair. [The Padilla affair was the episode that fractured the relationship between the Cuban Revolution and much of the international left-wing intelligentsia. Heberto Padilla, a poet who had supported the revolution but who turned to criticizing it in the late 1960s, saw his poetry collection Fuera del juego ( Out of the Game ) — awarded a prize by UNEAC in 1968 — published with a prologue branding it counterrevolutionary. In March 1971, he was arrested and jailed for just over a month, emerging only after reading a humiliating self-criticism before UNEAC in which he accused himself and other writers, a gesture that reminded many of Joseph Stalin’s Moscow show trials. The reaction was immediate: figures such as Jean-Paul Sartre, Simone du Beauvoir, Mario Vargas Llosa, Julio Cortázar, Susan Sontag, and Octavio Paz signed letters of protest, and the episode opened a schism in the cultural left and foreshadowed the hardening of the so-called Quinquenio Gris , the gray five-year period.] Abel Prieto The so-called Padilla affair. We made fools of ourselves and broadcast it to the whole world: Herberto Padilla’s self-criticism was a caricature of the traps of the Moscow trials. It was a grave mistake, one in which UNEAC, the Ministry of the Interior, and the Communist Party all took part. After the Padilla affair, great European intellectuals — even Sartre and Simone de Beauvoir — broke with Cuba. I think we were deceived. Padilla was an excellent poet, and I think we have to go on publishing him and, at the same time, make known an account of what really happened. Simón Vázquez There were also very harsh stretches, like the Military Units to Aid Production (UMAP) — military units that herded together religious believers, pacifists, and gay men into forced-labor camps in agriculture. Abel Prieto The stance we took toward gay people had several moments of repression. The infamous UMAP. . . . On Fidel and Raúl’s instructions, an investigation was carried out, because [there was a belief] that a homosexual who worked the land would “man up,” that he’d turn into a tough guy if you handed him a hoe and a machete. It’s absurd. All of that coincided with those currents of universal homophobia, the hormone-injection kind — like the case of Alan Turing, for example. Simón Vázquez You like to joke that you’re a “Marxist-Lennonist,” after John Lennon, and you claim the British artist as part of the revolution’s heritage. Abel Prieto Every time I post images on social media of Fidel at the Lennon monument in Havana, people pile on the hate, but they hate me even more intensely when I try to reclaim Lennon as part of the heritage of the Cuban Revolution. Lennon, an agent of empire? A revolutionary, absolutely! He backed every cause, against the Vietnam War, and he helped us. It’s madness that, out of clumsiness, we weren’t consistent about spreading the best of Lennon’s music and of authentic rock; instead there was a tendency to flee from English, “the language of the enemy.” That was my battle at the university: long hair, seed necklaces — the Cuban barbudos brought that into the twentieth century; the hippies imitated that symbol of rebellion of ours, not the other way around. How can we call a foreign affectation a symbol that we Cubans ourselves brought into the modern world? Simón Vázquez In your outlook, there’s an idea that becomes urgent today: that we face a confrontation between humanism and barbarism, trying to “salvage what we can” of humanity. Abel Prieto Life, people, the right to live. Simón Vázquez I’d like you to talk about that syncretism, that construction of socialism in the Caribbean, joining together elements that in a dogmatic phase might have been seen as utterly divergent. Abel Prieto At the beginning of the revolution, there were courses in scientific atheism; if you’d had your child baptized you couldn’t join the Communist Party, and neither could you if you’d married in the church: a phase of searching for a kind of ideological purity. That changed. A turning point was Frei Betto’s interview with Fidel, Fidel and Religion , which changed us Cubans and, more broadly, changed the way the revolutionary movement in Latin America looked at religion. Simón Vázquez And today? Abel Prieto It’s not possible to abandon the spiritual dimension, the religiosity of human beings; it’s not possible to leave man — as Sartre said — facing death, facing the void, facing nothingness. Revolutionary processes have to take that into account and integrate it. The besieged-fortress mentality, which has often done us harm, never led us to reject Cuban Santería, the Regla de Palo Monte, the Babalawos , the Abakuá , or the spiritists. Cuban spiritism is revolutionary. And the Family Code is a model of the vanguard: marriage equality, the right to adopt children. The evangelicals managed to muster a bloc of no votes against the code, but a great battle was won.

articles.title: Cori Bush Hopes to Extend the Black Radical Tradition
articles.author: Democratic Left
articles.content: Bush is fighting to reclaim a seat in the U.S. House that was lost to a historic barrage of cash in 2024. Election day in Missouri is Aug. 4. The post Cori Bush Hopes to Extend the Black Radical Tradition appeared first on Democratic Left .

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed Is In a Fight to Transform the Democratic Party
articles.content: Tuesday’s Democratic primary for the open U.S. Senate seat in Michigan is a national story, and not only because Michigan and Maine are likely to determine which party controls the upper chamber of Congress come January. The race between public health official Dr. Abdul El-Sayed and four-term U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens is also a microcosm of the struggle for the future of the Democratic Party — the war of position between progressives and centrists that is playing out all over the country. Last week I went to Metro Detroit and spent a few days talking with a range of people about this pivotal race. I was especially curious to explore the political dynamics in Michigan’s Jewish and Black communities, two voting blocks that could prove crucial in this contest. The outsize role of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) in the race has been widely discussed: AIPAC and affiliated groups have spent nearly $ 30 million in support of Stevens — their biggest investment ever in a single race. And the overall spending picture is extremely lopsided, with the Stevens campaign spending 12 times more than El-Sayed’s. AIPAC is, of course, hell-bent on defeating El-Sayed because of his critical stance on U.S. support for Israel. But the candidate doesn’t lead with Israel-Palestine or even bring it up much. His focus is decidedly domestic, as reflected in his campaign slogan: ​ “ Money Out of Politics. Money in Your Pocket. Medicare for All.” (Medicare for All has been a signature issue for El-Sayed going back several years. It was the centerpiece of his unsuccessful 2018 run for Michigan governor, and he co-authored a ​ “ citizen’s guide” on the subject, published in 2021 .) El-Sayed approaches Israel as a ​ “ kitchen table” issue. ​ “ Israel is an affordability issue,” he said in a recent interview with the journalist Anand Giridharadas. ​ “ Maybe we should keep our money here instead of sending it there to drop bombs on people’s schools or their hospitals. That’s our money. … And you want to send my money over there? That’s insane.” When Giridharadas noted that some have described this outlook as ​ “ America first from the left,” El-Sayed responded enthusiastically. ​ “ I have no problem saying America first. Yes, America first,” he said. He doesn’t limit this to Israel. ​ “ I don’t think Egypt should get any foreign military aid either, or Jordan or Pakistan or Saudi Arabia or the United Arab Emirates or Qatar,” he recently said in a podcast interview. What has received far less attention than AIPAC’s crusade against the Egyptian American is the considerable Jewish support he enjoys in Michigan. Last week I met with several Jewish supporters of El-Sayed’s campaign in the Metro Detroit area. One of those supporters, Don Greenspon, is a 76 -year-old attorney who resides in the heavily Jewish Detroit suburb of Huntington Woods. He is one of the co-founders of Jews for Abdul, a group that pushes back on the barrage of attacks against El-Sayed. Those attacks have traction in large swaths of the Jewish community, Greenspon said. But, he noted, the attacks tend not to focus on Israel, because El-Sayed’s detractors know that his views on that subject are increasingly popular among Democrats, especially younger ones. Instead, they attack him for having the controversial leftist streamer Hasan Piker as a surrogate. (Though support for El-Sayed actually increased after attack ads focused on Piker.) On Sunday, Jews for Abdul joined forces with Muslims for Abdul and Women for Abdul for a day of canvassing throughout neighborhoods in Detroit and Highland Park. They paired up into groups of two or three, with a Jew and a Muslim together in each group. ​ “ We canvassed together to show our solidarity with one another and to show that Abdul’s campaign represents people from all religions and walks of life,” Greenspon said. Ruqaya Ali of Muslims for Abdul and Steve Gold and Don Greenspon of Jews for Abdul in Midtown Detroit during a day of canvassing for Abdul El-Sayed’s U.S. Senate campaign in Michigan, July 26, 2026. (Courtesy of Muslims for Abdul and Jews for Abdul) Jess Newman is a 39 -year-old El-Sayed supporter who lives in the Detroit suburb of Ferndale and serves on the town’s local school board. The issue of Israel ​ “ is holding this campaign hostage,” she told me at a coffee shop last week. Newman grew up in what she describes as a ​ “ very Zionist community” in West Bloomfield, a suburb of Detroit. She worked for AIPAC at one point and is now active with Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). The ​ “ propaganda” against El-Sayed in the Jewish community, Newman said, has been so intense that it has created something of an ​ “ alternative universe” in which many Jews believe, for example, that El-Sayed wants all Jews dead. Her view is the exact opposite: El-Sayed is the only person in the race ​ “ who wants to keep my people safe.” It was a three-way race until one of the candidates, Mallory McMorrow, a member of the Michigan Senate, dropped out in early July. McMorrow had positioned herself somewhere between Stevens in the center and Abdul El-Sayed on the left, but found that her campaign wasn’t getting enough traction and withdrew. How McMorrow’s erstwhile supporters vote in Tuesday’s primary may determine the outcome. One of those McMorrow supporters, 57 -year-old Pamela Aronson, was undecided when I sat down with her to discuss the race a few days ago in the Detroit suburb of Huntington Woods, where she lives. Aronson teaches sociology at the University of Michigan-Dearborn. She co-authored the 2023 book Gender Revolution: How Electoral Politics and #MeToo Are Reshaping Everyday Life and two recent research papers on the ​ “ gender self-presentations” of women candidates for office. Aronson especially appreciated McMorrow’s strong advocacy of LGBTQ+ rights. The state senator’s withdrawal from the race left Aronson somewhat adrift and torn. She finds the deluge of attack ads from both Stevens and Abdul El-Sayed confounding. One such ad implied that El-Sayed was soft on antisemitism. Another accused El-Sayed of ​ “ a pattern of disrespecting women.” Aronson researched the claims and found that the quotes in question were taken ​ “ completely out of context” and ​ “ grasping at straws.” But most of the people such ads reach ​ “ aren’t going to go and look it up,” she said. (Rima Mohammad, a trustee on the Ann Arbor Public Schools Board of Education, has denounced the advertising campaign as racist and Islamophobic. ​ “ It is very anti-Muslim,” she recently said on a Michigan TV show.) On the other hand, Aronson said there’s part of her that’s ​ “ ready to just vote for a candidate because they’re a woman.” Although only 14 % of Michiganders are African-American, the community comprises close to a fifth of the state’s Democratic primary voters, and polls show Haley Stevens with a dramatic lead over Abdul El-Sayed among Black voters in Michigan. One recent poll shows 67 % of Black Democrats supporting Stevens and only 21 % supporting El-Sayed. This discrepancy is typically attributed to Stevens’ association with the Obama administration, in which she served as chief of staff for the U.S. Auto Rescue Task Force — a particularly salient role in Michigan, where the auto industry has long loomed large. Stevens worked under ​ “ car czar” Steven Rattner, who oversaw the Obama administration’s bailout of the Big Three U.S. automakers amid the 2008 - 2009 financial meltdown. (El-Sayed has the endorsement of the United Auto Workers, the largest labor union in Michigan.) The Stevens campaign has leaned into this Obama connection heavily, especially with Black voters. The airwaves have been awash with pro-Stevens ads featuring Barack and Michelle Obama. Critics say those ads are dishonest, as the former president has not endorsed Stevens in the primary. Vincent Hutchings, a professor of political science and Afroamerican Studies at the University of Michigan and author of Public Opinion and Democratic Accountability: How Citizens Learn About Politics , sees this ​ “ clever but somewhat misleading” identification with Obama as a key factor driving her support with Black voters — along with her name recognition and her assertion that El-Sayed didn’t support Kamala Harris in 2024 . In an ad, Stevens has accused El-Sayed of referring to the Harris campaign as ​ “ nauseating.” These claims require some unpacking. El-Sayed was a supporter of the ​ “ uncommitted” movement, which advocated withholding support for then-President Joe Biden in the 2024 Democratic primaries over his administration’s handling of the Gaza War. It wasn’t an outright refusal to vote for Biden in the general election, but an attempt to pressure him to change course on the war. As my colleague Samer Badawi reported at the time, Michigan was the nerve center of the ​ “ uncommitted” movement. But El-Sayed did endorse Harris for president when she became the nominee after Biden withdrew from the race. ​ “ Considering the dangers of the Republican nominee, & potential of her leadership, it’s time for all of us to unite behind @KamalaHarris to defeat Trump,” he wrote on social media. El-Sayed didn’t call Harris herself ​ “ nauseating”; he was commenting on the juxtaposition of the Harris-Walz campaign’s ​ “ joyful warriors” branding and the colossal destruction in Gaza. “ Watching elders who look like your parents, children who look like your kids, be pulled in parts out of rubble for a year, and then watching the split screen of this manufactured campaign of joy on behalf of Democrats was nauseating,” El-Sayed said in a November 2024 conference. But such nuances are hard to convey amid the war of narratives and the rough-and-tumble of a political campaign. The mere insinuation that El-Sayed failed to support Harris or spoke disparagingly about her could be enough to hurt him among Black Democrats. ​ “ The fact that he feels the need to defend himself on that position is an indication that he or his handlers thinks that he’s weak on it,” Hutchings said. Hutchings cautions against the temptation to see a ​ “ deeper ideological message” at work, as many commentators do when they posit a supposedly broad preference among Black voters for centrist over progressive candidates — citing, for example, Biden outperforming Bernie Sanders with African-American voters in the 2020 Democratic primary. ​ “ That shouldn’t be interpreted as ​ ‘ they’re embracing conservatism’ or ​ ‘ they’re rejecting progressivism.’ I think that would be a mistake,” he said. The race has taken on an increasingly bitter tone in the final stretch. “ Most voters are not combing the websites of the candidates to figure out where they stand on the issues,” Hutchings said. ​ “ Voters are wildly inconsistent. The notion that they have some coherent ideological framework to their preferences is a mythology” — one that is by no means peculiar to African Americans, he adds. The race has taken on an increasingly bitter tone in the final stretch. Several Michiganders I spoke with expressed deep dismay about this. One question that looms over the primary is what supporters of the respective candidates will do in the general election in November. Will Stevens supporters vote for El-Sayed against the Republican nominee, Mike Rogers (who lost to Democrat Elissa Slotkin in 2024 by fewer than 20 , 000 votes)? By the same token, will El-Sayed voters vote for Stevens in November? How many will sit the election out? Newman will vote for Stevens if El-Sayed loses Tuesday. ​ “ I’m a tactical voter,” she said. Greenspon, in contrast, was torn. He says he has ​ “ voted for the lesser evil” in the past — Hillary Clinton in 2016 , Biden in 2020 , Harris in 2024 — but is not sure if he can do it anymore. Many El-Sayed supporters, himself included, ​ “ will be devastated” if their candidate loses the primary, especially after the intensity and ugliness of the attacks on him from the Stevens campaign and the Democratic Party establishment. This dilemma and ambivalence reflect the crossroads at which Democrats find themselves nationally. The recent victories of DSA-aligned candidates in New York , Pennsylvania and Colorado have sent the Democratic National Committee and centrists in the party into panic mode, desperate to keep this socialist wave at bay. Yet if this rising progressive tide is thwarted in Michigan, it could hurt the party’s prospects in November. El-Sayed has spoken to this. If a business-as-usual Democrat like Stevens wins the primary, he warned officials with the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee last year, ​ “ don’t be surprised if you get a repeat of 2024 ” — when a critical mass of Arab and Muslim voters and young progressives, indignant over Harris’ equivocations on the Gaza War, sat out the election. That may have cost Harris the crucial state of Michigan. The margins are razor thin and the stakes are very high. This story was first published at New Lines Magazine .

articles.title: Reflections on Austin DSA’s Field Trip to the Blanton Museum of Art
articles.author: Red Fault -- Austin DSA
articles.content: by Megan N Indian Myths and Legends: The Pleiades – The Creation – The Coming of the Chinigchinich – The Island of the Dead By Reuben Kadish The first piece I saw on the recent Austin DSA “field trip” to the Blanton Museum of Art was Indian Myths and Legends: The Pleiades – The Creation – The Coming of the Chinigchinich – The Island of the Dead (1937-41) by Reuben Kadish 1 . It wasn’t really fair to the rest of the works in the exhibit, to start off so strong. The blurb in the museum said he was born to immigrant parents from Kovno, or presently Lithuania. His Wikipedia page 2 adds the context that this land was under the Russian Empire at the time of his birth, and that his father had been a part of the General Jewish Labor Bund, a secular Jewish socialist party, before emigrating. Wikipedia does not mention his mother, Ida Saks, whose name I found from a biography website that seems to have been written by a descendent 3 . As an artist for the Works Progress Administration (WPA), Kadish made plans and sketched “studies” for as many as twenty murals, but only two were accepted and completed: Physical Growth of Man / History of Medicine (1936) 4 and Dissertation on Alchemy (1937) 5 . Both were heavily inspired by his time in Mexico with muralist David Alfaro Siqueiros. The museum label said he ascribed his rejections to their being “too flamboyant, too revolutionary, too this, too that.” Regardless, he still got paid for coming up with ideas. Artists hired for the WPA were salaried and paid by the week, not by commission or output. Left: Photograph of Dissertation on Alchemy (1937) by Reuben Kadish. Right: Photograph of a section of Physical Growth of Man/History of Medicine (1936) by Reuben Kadish and Philip Guston. Among those flamboyant and revolutionary rejections was Indian Myths and Legends . I’m a sucker for anything with space references in it. The Pleiades is a star cluster that has six stars visible to the unaided, 20/20 eye; seven, if you are atop a mountain with perfectly clear skies and a new moon; and over a thousand stars if you have a telescope to help you out. The Western understanding of the Pleiades as the “Seven Sisters” comes from Greek mythology, as many of our astronomical names do. The Greek story involves young women, all mothers, who were fleeing the hunter Orion (a nearby constellation) who relentlessly pursued them for their beauty. It’s one of the myths that’s strikingly similar across the world. Kadish lived in southern California for most of his life, where the Payómkawichum (Luiseño) and Tongva (Gabrieliño, Fernandeño) 6 peoples understood the Pleiades as women escaping death by retreating to the skies. I could not find why the women were fleeing death in the Payómkawichum version, but they do so via a rope, and they cut the rope while a man is trailing behind them. He ends up as a bright star separate from the Pleiades, in the constellation we know as Taurus 7 . In the Tongva tale, the women “found out their partners were holding back food from the community” and catapulted themselves into space. One of the men came back home with food for his partner after all, and loved her so much that he, too, rushed to the skies, becoming the entirety of Taurus 8 . Kadish’s representation sits six cave-like drawings of bodies at the center-left on a gray background, with two more to the right, these separated on a blue background and sitting just underneath a large red-and-black body that I presume represents the men in the stories who followed the women into space, lagging just behind. How curious that the Pleiades cluster, visible from most of Earth in the winter as long as you’re not at the South Pole, has been so universally perceived as women, let alone as runaways and escape artists. The stories almost certainly predate ancient Greece 9 . Kadish’s depiction mostly evades gender, but I don’t know if the work would have struck me in the same way without its amorphous bodies swimming alongside the fish, without the sharp skeletons dancing on their postmortem island. I found no history or analysis of this piece online. I wonder from whom he heard these stories, and what he hoped to convey to Americans had it become a WPA-sponsored mural after all. Kadish’s political convictions were no secret; he and Philip Guston are responsible for a mural in Mexico so momentous that it has multiple names (though I favor The Struggle against War and Fascism ). The mural had to be hidden behind a fake wall for three decades after being deemed offensive by the Catholic Church. Both men were also targeted by the Los Angeles police’s “Red Squads” for making art with the Marxist-affiliated John Reed Clubs to protest the racist trial of the Scottsboro Boys 10 . The LAPD didn’t just destroy a dozen paintings, they shot at the people depicted in each one. Kadish was already familiar with this kind of persecution: his childhood home had been ransacked for his father’s “Bolshevik sympathies.” He continually spoke about worker’s rights and the abolition of class in interviews throughout his life. Why the artistic focus on indigenous mythology? In 1943, not long after his stint with the WPA, Kadish was recruited to document the war as an Army artist. In an interview conducted with Kadish a few months before his passing in 1992, he had this to say about the impact of the war on his art: “Well, you can’t have the impact of the horrendousness of the kind of death that the world had seen without asking yourself some questions as to where we came from and where do we think we’re going, and who’s your mother and who’s your father, and who do you think you can choose to find in this world of ours? … In all religions, and when we read the [stories] that seem to be most gratifying … they’re the ones that we least understand. They’re the ones that have more poetic elements in them, that carry out more than just the fringe of what a mother figure is all about.” 11 But Indian Myths was made before Kadish had seen that “kind of death” up close in a war. He was clearly thinking about storytelling, creation, and loss before then. Did he witness another kind of death in his youth that compelled his interest in these themes? Political repression and the police state followed him throughout his formative years. Yet his art highlighted the humanity of nearly everyone but himself. Kadish chose solidarity, reminding us that we achieve universal dreams of peace and livelihood by working as a collective, that disconnected people across the world can look at a blurry patch of sky and see the same vision. Works Cited https://blanton.emuseum.com/objects/21172/ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reuben_Kadish https://kadishart.org/biography-reuben/ https://livingnewdeal.org/sites/city-of-hope-guston-and-kadish-mural-duarte-ca/ https://digitalcollections.sdsu.edu/do/814f8546-f84f-41bc-9082-74c4f41b1af4 I only provided the Spanish-given names to make one’s independent research easier, as I found these names were used more often in text. https://www.caltech.edu/about/news/before-the-telescope https://www.lacountyarts.org/experiences/civic-art/memory-and-futurity-yaangna https://theconversation.com/the-worlds-oldest-story-astronomers-say-global-myths-about-seven-sisters-stars-may-reach-back-100-000-years-151568 https://reubenkadish.org/publication/double-consciousness-in-mexico/ https://www.aaa.si.edu/collections/interviews/oral-history-interview-reuben-kadish-12170 The post Reflections on Austin DSA’s Field Trip to the Blanton Museum of Art first appeared on Red Fault .

articles.title: To Care for the Sick: Thoughts of an ICU RN
articles.author: Red Fault -- Austin DSA
articles.content: By Asanti M We will all be sick, but we will not all receive care. Our mortality guarantees the former, but it is the system, chosen for us, that forces us to cope with the latter. For the unempathetic or short-sighted among us, the latter is a sad fact, but one not worthy of any recourse. They see themselves as happily positioned to receive their care and don’t dare dream that they will ever count themselves among the sick. To them, there exists a stark separation between those who will and who won’t receive healthcare: the deserving and the listless, the good and the wicked, so on and so forth. Whatever rationale is necessary to obfuscate the human condition of ailment is employed to justify a perverse system. The collective effort to care for the sick stands as a testament to the inherent communal nature of human life in which two important points ought to be discerned. First, there’s recognition of the necessity of communal bonds. To organize and use resources on the impaired as opposed to the healthy suggests either a strong utility to gain from the health of others, or an emotional bend towards the preservation of another that surpasses the expense necessary to care for them. Of course, both can be true at once. Second, ailment is a universality embedded in the human condition in which we all can empathetically enter, to some degree. Therefore, some semblance of systematic healthcare that promotes communal health and safeguards the fragility of life naturally emerges as a joint effort to alleviate one’s own suffering. Healthcare, being an extension of communal relations and common sentiments, is then naturally positioned as a public good. The contortion of healthcare into a product sold solely to maximize monetary ends, fundamentally alters how we discuss and analyze the preservation of life. This peculiar transmutation yields the very sinister consequence in which callous indifference is amplified and allowed to tear apart the very basic ties of empathy. This virulent apathy numbs the public to the condemnation of our neighbors who are left to the selfish and subversive schemes of profiteers, whose existence is made entirely on maximizing public extraction. The conversation shifts from life and death, suffering and repose, to the economic jargon that surrounds the client-supplier model and wholly conceals the humanitarian gravity of such a callous approach. These profiteers move to restrict the communal aspect of healthcare fully ceding any semblance of its humanitarian nature until the sick and suffering become unwitting consumers. All talk of preservation of life loses meaning when the preservation of dividends supersedes its importance and constricts its application. The apathy elicited by the transformation of healthcare exists not solely as a natural byproduct of the commodification, but as a sought-after condition that must be met in order to maximize the profitability of suffering. Under the benign contentment of apathy, an all too familiar structure takes root. Executives are selected to manage funds and generate profits; administrators are hired to push efficiencies towards cost reduction; and managers enter as mediators between bureaucratic will and clinical expertise. With such a normative system in place it’s difficult to see the intrinsic contradictions that produce its disparities until we look among its victims. Far too many of us are forced to weigh the options of an agonizing abstinence, or seek care that thrust us into destitution. The hailed “market forces” drive the public to the upper limit of what they can afford at which point the invisible hand of the market becomes indistinguishable from the sordid hand of death. Both equally unfeeling and equally cold. The atmosphere of apathy transitions to a confused helplessness as the general public questions “how did we get here” and any answer provided sums up to “this is how things have to be”. With the inquisition underway, the public forcefully ascribes their poor conditions to a variety of pernicious players, accusing them of all manner of “rule breaking” leading to the degradation of the system. This line of thought mistakenly grants too much consequence and culpability to the disposition of individual players and fails to see the ghost in the machine, the invisible hand. To perform well in an environment bent on making profit is to shift efforts towards that end as demanded by competition or collusion, despite how scrupulous an individual might be. What results is a race yielding higher and higher costs of care, even if it means neglecting the preservation of life. This is not to say that any one profiteer acts as an exceptionally malevolent operator but acknowledges that their motives are entirely irrelevant when positioned within a system designed to commodify life and wellness. Competition rewarded based on the generation of revenue bends the health care industry towards extraction. Hospitals, insurance agencies, pharmaceuticals, medical device companies, medical coders, etc. all claw to extract as much wealth from the public as possible. This economic position is by no means unique, but when adopted by health care it’s difficult to distinguish lifesaving medical treatment from extortion. The makeup of such a system leaves culpability lost in its machinery. Employers move to stay alive in response to market forces and employees follow suit so as to not become victims themselves. Cornered clinicians are reduced to cogs, and whether ambivalent or begrudging, complicity becomes the defining mode of all components. Each piece turns independently towards their personal wellbeing, and in doing so inadvertently line the gears perfectly to perpetuate our Machiavellian healthcare machine. The life of our Frankenstein system requires close collusion between those who benefit from its monstrous design, and the absolute atomization of all who blindly grasp its contours with their hopes and fears in hand. Collective action is reserved for the corporate but fiercely condemned amongst the “consumers” and the “cogs”. Collusion at every junction of our system forces both prices and public confusion to outpace legislation as monopolies systematically tip the scale in their favor. It’s imperative that “consumers” remain impotent and assert no will that runs contrary towards the higher purpose of profit if healthcare is to exist solely as a commodity. The ideal consumer becomes both the perpetrator and the victim. Under the cloak of apathy, the national exaltation of the individual over the community begets an ecosystem ideal to undermine any step towards humanitarian solidarity. However, in true dialectical fashion, the conditions forced on the majority become a unifying factor, fomenting the prerequisites for change and tearing at the seams of apathy. The countless barriers to access once again make the inescapable nature of ailment front and center in the national consciousness. Through the lens of solidarity any system that forces such a cruel reality on far too many of us becomes criminal; the callous discussions surrounding human life become untenable; and the humanitarian position becomes emboldened. The unified potential of the uncared-for drives discussions both foreboding and inspiring as an opportunity to steer history emerges. Further Reading An American Sickness by Elisabeth Rosenthal Priced Out by Uwe E. Reinhardt The Tyranny of Merit: Can We Find the Common Good by Michael J. Sandel Evicted by Matthew Desmon The post To Care for the Sick: Thoughts of an ICU RN first appeared on Red Fault .

articles.title: Liberty’s Anniversary (1895)
articles.author: Rochester Red Star: News from Rochester DSA
articles.content: by Eugene V. Debs Eugene V. Debs (1855 – 1926) was a labor leader and socialist candidate for president. As president of the American Railway Union, Debs took part in the Pullman Strike. Debs was arrested when federal judges issued an injunction, and forces were dispatched to stop the strikes. Debs was sentenced to six months in jail, during which time he “began to read and think and dissect the anatomy of the system in which workingmen, however organized, could be shattered and battered and splintered at a single stroke,” and became a socialist. In the following excerpt [PDF] , published on July 4, Debs reflects on the supposed American liberties of our founding, and decries their betrayal in the “despotic decree” of the injunction. – GLH Sitting in Woodstock Jail, behind prison bars, and permitting my fancy to have free rein, what more natural than to contemplate the resounding acclamations of a great nation celebrating the anniversary of the birthday of Liberty? What more natural than to commune with the dead, who, when living, in the spirit of heroism expanded to the full stature of patriots and dared all things, battles, wounds, imprisonment, confiscation, and death, to secure liberty for themselves and their posterity. But in the midst of such ardent admiration of the men who wrested the scepter from England’s proud monarch and secured for the American people the priceless boon of liberty, I am compelled to ponder present conditions and ask myself, “What remains of the liberty thus secured for the American people? Why celebrate the ‘birthday’ of American liberty when Liberty itself lies cold and stiff and dead, stabbed to death by nine gowned and ermined men, who, if they have any mission connected with the affairs of the American people, it is to forever stand guard over their constitutional and unalienable rights.” It has been regarded as a patriotic duty for Americans, on the 4th of July, to apostrophize Liberty and to select from the vocabularies of all languages eulogistic words to describe its value and its glory, and when words failed to express those essential attributes of liberty which made life itself an inferior blessing, bonfires have blazed, cannons have belched their thunder, banners have waved, drums have throbbed, and bugle blasts have called the people to assemble and rejoice together over God’s inscrutable decree in bestowing upon Americans blessings denied to all other peoples, kindreds, and tongues since time began. Nor do I doubt that on this anniversary such exhibitions will be repeated, but it will be a hollow mockery. The stage will be gorgeous with scenery for the play of liberty, but liberty will be absent – only its ghost will appear, only its “canonized bones” will be present; only its skeleton jaws will move to tell American slaves that the supreme “funeral directors” have buried it in a potter’s field without so much as a slab to mark its resting place. And yet the farce will proceed, and orators will be found to bombard the air to convince the people that in the nation’s grand march across the continent and in its physical achievements, the ultima thule of its destiny has been reached. If liberty is referred to at all, it will be to emphasize the plutocratic doctrine that a government of the people, by the people, and for the people and constitutional guarantees of liberty are as so many vagaries and that a strong, centralized government is what the Fathers designed should be established upon the ruins of the Republic, and that the Constitution itself, ceasing to be a guarantee of the liberties of the people, should be eventually so construed that one man, robed, crowned, and sceptered as a judge, combining the characteristics of caitiff and satrap, could, as whim might influence him, strike down every constitutional right of the citizen and send him to prison. . . . If the anniversary of the 4th of July is devoted to arousing the American people to a realization of their great misfortune, if they will resolve to regain their liberties by renewing he pledge of the Fathers to perish or conquer, then Woods and Woodstock Jail may stand in the future monumental infamies, from which the people may go forth as did the revolutionary heroes from the infamous edicts of King George to regain their lost liberties – and all along the lines of the hosts of the common people, the victims of plutocracy and their corrupt agencies, should resound again the battle cry that was heard from Lexington to Yorktown: “Give me liberty or give me death!” The post Liberty’s Anniversary (1895) first appeared on Rochester Red Star .

articles.title: Bolivian Prosecutor’s Office issues arrest warrant for Evo Morales
articles.author: Pablo Meriguet
articles.content: On July 29, the Bolivian Public Prosecutor’s Office in Santa Cruz issued an arrest warrant against former leftist President Evo Morales (2006–2019). Authorities accuse Morales of having led the recent anti-government and anti-neoliberal protests that rocked Bolivia for more than 50 days. The specific charges against the Indigenous former president are terrorism, endangering the safety of transportation systems, criminal conspiracy, public incitement to commit a crime, endangering the safety of public services, and armed insurrection against the state. The prosecution is seeking between 20 and 30 years in prison for the alleged crimes of terrorism and armed insurrection alone. The prosecution claims that Morales is responsible for these actions allegedly because he participated in massive protests, during which demonstrators demanded the resignation of the newly-inaugurated president, right-wing Rodrigo Paz, for having introduced a neoliberal bill that allowed for the expropriation of land to settle debts (something that is prohibited in the country) among other things. The complaint that led to the issuance of an arrest warrant was initially filed by Stello Cochamanidis Garces and by the Interior Minister Marco Oviedo Huerta, who joined the complaint sometime later. Thus, the warrant states : “[Morales] must come forward to explain what his role was during the 53 days (of road blockades), to explain why he made the statements he did, why he took responsibility, and why he said that he was the one who was practically in charge of the actions.” Morales claims this is political persecution For his part, on his X account, Morales rejected the arrest warrant : “Today the government issued a new arrest warrant against me, accusing me of alleged crimes of terrorism and armed insurrection. They seek to hold us responsible for the social protests to hide the true tragedy Bolivia is facing: a deep economic and social crisis, the result of a model that has abandoned the people and protects corruption. Our position has always been clear: we stand with those suffering from austerity measures, fuel shortages, the rising cost of living, insecurity, and the spread of drug trafficking.” In addition, the former president said that neither he nor the Bolivians demanding change will be “intimidated”: “They won’t solve the problems they themselves have caused through legal proceedings and political persecution; they’re just trying to divert attention with a new headline … We will continue to fight alongside the people, as we have always done, with the conviction that Bolivia deserves a different path: one of dignity, sovereignty, social justice, and the restoration of hope for everyone.” It is not the first time that Morales is facing charges. In 2024, the Prosecutor’s Office issued an arrest warrant against him for the alleged crimes of human trafficking and smuggling, a warrant that (though categorically rejected by Morales) was renewed in 2025. The prosecutor’s office accuses him of having had a romantic relationship with a minor, something Morales has called “absurd”: “The only thing missing was for them to order my immediate dismemberment in a public square, as happened in the colonial era when the conquistadors severely punished Indigenous people who rebelled against oppression,” he said in 2025. However, the trial was halted because Morales didn’t show up for the hearings, claiming that the trial was flawed and designed to destroy him both politically and physically. It is speculated that he is in the Chapare region, in the department of Cochabamba, an area where thousands of peasants have vowed to defend him against any attempt to arrest him or take his life.

articles.title: Will Trump’s FBI arrest you for your social media posts?
articles.author: Rania Khalek
articles.content: Will Trump’s FBI arrest you for your social media posts? After NSPM-7, the federal agency is building a real-life Minority Report predictive policing system with AI. And millions of Americans could be at risk. Investigative reporter Daniel Boguslaw breaks down how the proposed FBI Threat Screening Center would use “predictive” artificial intelligence technology to expand its watch lists. Boguslaw’s reporting reveals a skyrocketing number of US citizens the Bureau is tracking, based on “foreign agent” designations laid out in NSPM-7’s broad criminalization of speech and political affiliation. But “predictive” crime systems don’t work: Boguslaw points to the Boston Marathon bomber, the Pulse nightclub shooter, and January 6 participants who were on the FBI’s watch list — even without AI. He says expanded surveillance isn’t a uniquely Trump-era threat, and that despite sitting members of Congress being blacklisted by Marco Rubio’s Cuba report, lawmakers on both sides aren’t doing enough to check the growing abuse of power. articles.title: Trump can’t defeat Iran – & the Pentagon knows it | w/ Mohammad Marandi
articles.author: Rania Khalek
articles.content: The US is losing the war in Iran and admitting it: Trump won’t force Tehran into submission or negotiation with airstrikes, now confirmed by the Pentagon and the CIA. As Dr. Mohammad Marandi of the University of Tehran tells Rania Khalek and Zoe Alexandra, the “bombing campaign in search of a strategy” and Washington’s strategic loss in this war have little to do with its ongoing shortage of interceptor missiles. He explains why Iran is targeting US/Israeli radar infrastructure across the Gulf, Iraq, and now Jordan, and unpacks how, after provoking Yemen, Saudi Arabia is stuck fighting a war it already lost once. And, debunking the myth of Iranian “proxies,” Marandi digs in to Ukraine’s CIA-backed attack on a cargo ship in the Caspian Sea – and what Tehran’s retaliation could mean for Russia’s long-term strategic position in the region. “The Iranians will continue to punish the United States until they get what they consider to be a just resolution to this problem, which may or may not be anytime soon.” Watch full episodes of BT Live, join breakthroughnews.org as a member today!

articles.title: Ecuador: la semi dictadura de Noboa busca ganar por eliminación de opositores, no por votos
articles.author: Pilar Troya Fernández
articles.content: Read in English here El presidente Daniel Noboa gobierna Ecuador con métodos cada vez más autoritarios. Elegido en 2023 y reelegido en 2025, ha concentrado poder en el Ejecutivo, chocado con la Corte Constitucional, abusado de los estados de excepción y convertido a la justicia en un instrumento contra sus adversarios. Analistas y organizaciones de derechos humanos describen una deriva filodictatorial: un mandatario que conserva las formas de la democracia mientras erosiona su contenido. La antesala de las elecciones de gobiernos locales del 29 de noviembre de 2026 ofrece el ejemplo más nítido de esa estrategia, dirigida a ganar con la estrategia de dejar sin candidaturas a la oposición. Una jugada en dos movimientos La maniobra combina dos piezas que solo se entienden juntas. La primera: el 6 de marzo de 2026, a partir de una denuncia de la Fiscalía, un juez del Tribunal Contencioso Electoral (TCE) suspendió por nueve meses a la Revolución Ciudadana (RC), el mayor partido opositor y movimiento del expresidente Rafael Correa. La medida fue ratificada semanas después y, en julio, avalada por la Corte Constitucional. Al mismo tiempo, Unidad Popular, partido de izquierda y Construye, movimiento de derecha por el que fue candidato presidencial Fernando Villavicencio, asesinado en 2023, fueron sacados del registro de organizaciones políticas por el Consejo Nacional Electoral (CNE) con el argumento de que no cumplían el número mínimo de afiliados que exige la ley. La apelación fue negada en el caso de Construye que denunció una “persecución judicial a críticos y opositores” y calificó la decisión de fraude democrático. Unidad Popular consiguió probar que el CNE actuó fuera del límite temporal legal (23 días tarde), y que la cancelación carecía de respaldo suficiente sobre el número real de afiliados. La segunda pieza es el calendario. En marzo, el Consejo Nacional Electoral (CNE) adelantó al 29 de noviembre de 2026 las elecciones de gobiernos locales previstas para febrero de 2027, alegando el riesgo de lluvias del Fenómeno del Niño; ni el Niño de 1998 ni la pandemia habían justificado antes un adelanto semejante. El efecto de encajar ambas piezas es preciso: el nuevo periodo de inscripción de candidaturas – del 2 al 17 de agosto de 2026 – cae dentro de los nueve meses en que la oposición está suspendida. Adelantar las elecciones para hacerlas coincidir con la suspensión impide que el principal rival del gobierno (RC) presente listas con su propia sigla. El partido alternativo, también clausurado Ante el bloqueo, el correísmo buscó una salida legal: inscribir a sus candidatos bajo el movimiento aliado Amigo. La alternativa duró poco. El 16 de julio, la Fiscalía informó al TCE de una investigación por presunto lavado de activos contra ese movimiento; al día siguiente, el Tribunal lo suspendió también por nueve meses, y el CNE ejecutó la medida de inmediato, apenas dos semanas antes del plazo de inscripción. La conducta del Ejecutivo alimenta las sospechas. El 23 de julio, Noboa afirmó que los precandidatos podían inscribirse por “cualquier otro partido que no se haya prestado para lavado de activos”, mencionando al Partido Socialista a la par, o sea presentando como hecho consumado un presunto delito que aún se investiga. Su secretario de la Administración Pública, José Julio Neira, exdirector de la unidad estatal que maneja la información financiera reservada, detalló en público el origen de las sospechas. El jurista Mauricio Alarcón advirtió que lo alarmante no es la investigación, sino que el gobierno parezca conocer expedientes reservados “que ni siquiera están en manos de los actores afectados”, y cuestionó “la selectividad” y la coincidencia con el calendario electoral. Si los candidatos de la RC se inscriben por el Partido Socialista, no sorprendería que este fuera también cancelado o suspendido. Tortura, desapariciones y activistas muertos Todo ocurre sobre un telón de fondo siniestro. En junio de 2026, Ecuador ingresó por primera vez en el Índice Global de Tortura de la Organización Mundial Contra la Tortura, en la categoría de “alto riesgo”: la entidad documentó 369 denuncias de tortura y al menos 51 desapariciones forzadas atribuidas a agentes estatales entre 2024 y 2026, en el marco del “conflicto armado interno” declarado por el gobierno, mismo que ha decretado 21 estados de excepción, 9 toques de queda y 272 días con restricción de movimientos con resultado casi nulo en reducción de la criminalidad y un aumento del desplazamiento interno por amenazas, extorsión y presiones de los grupos criminales. En ese clima se inscriben dos muertes. Robinson del Pezo, que cubría conflictos de tierras en la provincia de Santa Elena, fue asesinado en noviembre de 2025. La activista anticorrupción Mónica Silva, de origen polaco y radicada más de una década en el país, que había exigido justicia por ese crimen y denunciado amenazas contra su vida, fue hallada muerta el 8 de junio de 2026. El ministro del Interior sugirió un suicidio, pero la autopsia reveló un golpe en la cabeza y estrangulamiento. Silva investigaba presuntos envíos de cocaína ocultos en contenedores de banano de una empresa vinculada a la familia del presidente, y una red de tráfico de tierras. La relatora de la ONU para defensores de derechos humanos pidió a Ecuador “cesar la persecución” y proteger a los activistas. Corrupción casa adentro El discurso oficial presenta las causas contra la oposición como una cruzada anticorrupción. Sin embargo, el mayor escándalo del periodo salpica al propio Ejecutivo: en el caso Progen, la Contraloría General del Estado cifró en unos 104 millones de dólares el perjuicio al Estado por contratos de generación térmica de emergencia firmados en 2024 con esa empresa estadounidense, cuyos equipos nunca entraron en operación. Están además los ocho cargamentos de cocaína encontrados en las exportaciones de banano de la familia Noboa. El resultado es una elección cuyos contendientes se definen en los tribunales antes que en las urnas. El gobierno insiste en que se trata de causas ajenas al Ejecutivo; la oposición y parte de la comunidad jurídica replican que la selectividad de los procesos y su oportuno calendario apuntan en otra dirección. Pilar Troya Fernández es ecuatoriana, antropóloga con maestría en estudios de género e investigadora del Instituto Tricontinental de Investigación Social . Fue asesora de la Secretaría Nacional de Planificación, asesora de la Secretaría Nacional de Educación Superior, Ciencia, Tecnología e Innovación y Subsecretaria General de Educación Superior en Ecuador. Actualmente reside en Brasil. Este artículo fue producido por Globetrotter .
